title: UCC Milk Coffee launched in 1969. Why was convenience still so hard? | Brand Stories
description:
What work must happen before you can drink a can of milk coffee on the go? Follow this UCC product from prototypes around 1968 and its 1969 launch to deliveries at Osaka Expo 1970, then see how holes were actually made in the original can. Historical and technical accounts are attributed to the maker and interviewees. The earlier Mira example is distinguished from the milk-containing claim. Visuals are original anonymous concept illustrations.

c11r1h01.text: If it were your little shop, would you give three cases of milk coffee some shelf space?

c11r1h02.text: Tatsushi Ueshima later recalled salespeople entering food shops to sell UCC Milk Coffee, launched in 1969.

c11r1h03.text: I hadn't expected this side of convenience: once you make the can, someone still has to let it into their shop.

c11r1h04.text: How could the milk stay mixed inside the can?

c11h04b1.text: And how could cold cans keep up with the crowds at the Expo?

c11r1h05.text: Follow this UCC milk coffee through factories and the Expo in the two years around its launch, to find what else portability required.

c11r1h06.text: Once a coffee leaves the shop, what lets you enjoy the whole drink somewhere else?

c11r1o01.text: First, it had to leave the returnable bottle behind. UCC later recounted that its founder, Tadao Ueshima, once bought bottled coffee with milk at a station.

c11r1o02.text: The departure bell rang. Before he had finished, he had to return the bottle to the stall and hurry onto the train.

c11r1o03.text: You paid for the drink, but its container limited your time to drink it. When it was time to leave, that last sip had to stay behind.

c11r1o04.text: In a later interview, Tatsushi Ueshima described another transport problem with glass bottles: they were heavy, and breakage could be dangerous.

c11r1o06.text: Sealing milk coffee in a can you needn't return became the direction. But had coffee really never been canned before?

c11r1o07.text: Hamada City's records say Mira Coffee was already on sale at the Nihombashi Mitsukoshi main store on September 14, 1965.

c11r1o08.text: A later industry interview described Mira as sweetened coffee without milk. This UCC prototype would put milk in as well.

c11r1o09.text: UCC's museum calls its own product the world's first canned coffee containing milk. That is the museum's description of its own product.

c11r1o10.text: What I want to know is whether coffee and milk could stay properly mixed once sealed inside a can.

c11r1o11.text: In an interview, UCC's museum director placed the start of development around 1968, with a company project formed to pursue it.

c11r1o12.text: If you stood beside the prototype table, you would face more than a change of container: coffee and milk had to go inside together.

c11r1o13.text: At the moment you mix them, they can look much like a cup of milk coffee. The new difficulty appears after they go into the can.

c11r1o14.text: How could the milk in the can stay in that mixed state?

c11r1t01.text: A later interview report says that after coffee extract and milk were mixed and canned, milk components would separate and rise to the top.

c11r1t04.text: So how could the act of mixing produce something that stayed mixed?

c11r1t05.text: The interview described making the milk particles uniform, using homogenization to suppress separation.

c11r1t06.text: Only when I read about this step did I realize the team was working on a liquid state you don't normally watch closely.

c11r1t07.text: You wouldn't inspect tiny particles before buying a can of milk coffee. The people making the drink have to do that work first.

c11r1t08.text: But once the milk stops rising, is the drink ready to hand over?

c11r1t09.text: There was also heating. The maker later explained that high-temperature sterilization changes coffee's flavor and creates unwanted heated odors.

c11r1t10.text: Milk coffee must be sterilized, yet the person drinking it still judges with their tongue whether it tastes right.

c11r1t11.text: At a table, you can add milk if the coffee tastes too bitter. Inside a sealed can, the flavor must be settled before you open it.

c11r1t12.text: What could they use to keep adjusting the flavor after heating?

c11r1t13.text: The report says they kept tasting prototypes, seeking the proportions of coffee, milk and sugar that would reduce the flavor left by heating.

c11r1t16.text: Once the liquid was adjusted, was the outer shell merely there to hold it?

c11r1w01.text: The metal can played a part too. UCC later said iron ions inside the can would combine with components in the coffee.

c11r1w02.text: The maker named that component as tannin. After the reaction, the milk coffee would turn very dark.

c11r1w03.text: You think the shell only makes it easy to carry. Now it could even alter what the drink looks like.

c11r1w04.text: This time, the change had to be inside the can. Who could separate the coffee from that layer of metal?

c11r1w05.text: UCC says it worked with a can manufacturer to develop technology for applying a special coating inside the can.

c11r1w06.text: That treatment addressed discoloration caused by the can wall, keeping coffee from direct contact with bare metal.

c11r1w07.text: What interests me is that designing milk coffee to go eventually meant changing how the packaging was made too.

c11r1w10.text: The maker records that sales began in April. But would anyone buy a can and take it away from where they usually drank coffee?

c11r1w11.text: In a Guinness World Records interview, Tatsushi Ueshima recalled that some in the industry initially regarded canned coffee as heresy.

c11r1w17.text: The interviewee said some shopkeepers agreed to stock it after tasting it. That first sip came before its place on the shelf.

c11r1w12.text: Did anyone reorder after those first few cases entered food shops?

c11r1w14.text: The interviewee said orders gradually grew from ten cases to thirty. The cans found their way into shops little by little.

c11r1w15.text: You originally went into a food shop for familiar things. Putting the new can there gave it a chance to be picked up.

c11r1w16.text: But selling in a few shops was one thing. How could more people on the move discover this way of drinking coffee?

c11r1s01.text: The maker later recalled salespeople loudly asking for the product by name at station shops, then taking the cans they bought onto trains.

c11r1s02.text: The interview also records them lining up several cans by train windows so other passengers could see them.

c11r1s03.text: Among the products you could see in the carriage was a shape unlike a coffee cup. The can became display space too.

c11r1s04.text: I find this a small but fitting action: to convince people it could travel, they had to take it traveling.

c11r1s05.text: Yet that promotion didn't make it familiar overnight. Where could people from many places encounter the same can of milk coffee?

c11r1s19.text: An interview report says that when UCC began preparing for Expo business, it initially had little sense of the event's scale.

c11r1s20.text: At one point, people in the company imagined about 100,000 visitors. Would that estimate hold when managers went to look for themselves?

c11r1s21.text: Managers inspected overseas and found a scale far beyond their initial expectations, so they brought the Expo into their sales strategy.

c11r1s06.text: The following March, the Japan World Exposition opened in Osaka. A product previously introduced shop by shop gained another place to meet customers.

c11r1s07.text: UCC's museum director later said in an interview that they used their links with coffee-producing countries to contact participating nations.

c11r1s08.text: Coffee shops and dining spaces in the pavilions needed supplies. UCC's existing coffee business now came into play.

c11r1s09.text: But securing a supply opportunity doesn't deliver a cold can to a stall by itself. Where would cans connect to the Expo site?

c11r1s10.text: They set up the Osaka North Branch beside the Osaka manufacturing plant. At the time, it was also called the Expo Branch.

c11r1s11.text: Milk coffee was chilled at this distribution base before trucks took it to the site. The interview says several vehicles were prepared for this.

c11r1s13.text: I'm more curious about how people outside the Expo would hear about this milk coffee.

c11r1s14.text: Visitors at the site began picking up the canned drink. Period photos preserved by the maker also show cans of milk coffee in people's hands.

c11r1s15.text: People from different places took their experience home. News of the drink traveled beyond the Expo with them.

c11r1s16.text: The interview also says television brought images of visitors holding cans into homes, reaching people who hadn't been there.

c11r1s17.text: Later, inquiries and orders poured in. Even sales channels that had previously ignored this milk coffee began asking for stock.

c11r1s18.text: If more people want stock, does that mean enough stock can be made?

c11r1d01.text: The maker recalls that demand grew stronger in summer. Even producing at full capacity, the factory couldn't keep up.

c11r1d02.text: A UCC manager said in an interview that trucks waited outside the factory so products could leave as soon as they were made.

c11r1d03.text: You buy one can, but distribution must collect batch after batch. The extra demand ultimately arrived at the factory gate.

c11r1d04.text: I think this is where you feel the weight of delivery: people ready to drink had appeared, and the makers still had to catch up.

c11r1d05.text: When one factory couldn't supply enough, how could they fill the gap?

c11r1d06.text: The interview records the company expanding its network of partner factories across regions, so supply no longer depended on the original plant alone.

c11r1d07.text: Tatsushi Ueshima's recollection also lists adoption by the Railway Welfare Association as a turning point, giving the milk coffee a route to more travelers.

c11r1d09.text: And when you reached a sales counter and actually picked up that original can, one small action still remained.

c11r1d11.text: The maker's description of the original can says to pierce its top with a dedicated opener. What did those holes each do?

c11r1d12.text: One was for drinking, the other for air. To use them, you still needed a tool that could open those passages.

c11r1d13.text: The pull-open-and-drink action you're familiar with today wasn't something fingers alone could accomplish on that can top.

c11r1ct1.text: This milk coffee carried coffee drinking beyond its usual place, but it didn't remove the work of getting the drink to you. That work went into manufacturing, distribution and the can top.

c11r1ct2.text: Do you remember your first canned drink? Did someone open it for you, or did you open it yourself? Tell me in the comments.

c11r1ct3.text: To see how familiar objects put convenience in your hands, subscribe and explore the choices behind those small actions with me.
